explanations.explanation: The psalm says it plainly: "The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the distant shores be glad." The King is on the throne, and the invitation is to gladness. Notice the far-off shores get invited too, not just the folks sitting close to the action. Even the farthest coastline gets a seat at this celebration.

I get the pick, friend. A King on the throne sounds like a hush-and-bow moment. But the psalm says "…let the earth rejoice; let the distant shores be glad." That's a call to gladness, and nothing in it says to bow or be silent.

Hiding makes sense if you think a throne room means trouble. Here's what the singer actually says: "…let the earth rejoice; let the distant shores be glad." Nobody is told to duck behind the flour sacks. The call goes out to the whole earth to be glad.

Verse 2 says it: "righteousness and justice are His throne’s foundation." The clouds and darkness are around Him, but what the throne stands on is righteousness and justice. Think of a cookie stack that never wobbles because the bottom layer is solid. That's the base, and everything else sits on it.

Strength and splendor sound like throne-room words, so I see why you grabbed them. But the psalm names something else under the throne: "righteousness and justice…" Those are the foundation. Splendor might look great on top, friend, but the foundation is what holds everything up.

With clouds, darkness and all that drama, fear and might feels like a fair guess. The psalm says the throne's foundation is "righteousness and justice…" That's what it's built on. The clouds are around Him, and the justice is under Him.

Verse 3 says, "Fire goes before Him and consumes His foes on every side." The fire goes ahead of Him, and it reaches His foes on every side. I know that's a heavy line, so it's worth sitting with it for a second. You read it right.

This one is actually true. The psalm says, "Fire goes before Him and consumes His foes on every side." It goes before Him, and it reaches His foes on every side. I know that's a heavy line, so it's worth sitting with it for a second.

Verse 4 says, "His lightning illuminates the world; the earth sees and trembles." The earth sees the light, and it trembles. I think I'd be shaking right along with it, like my mustache when I forget the oven timer and hear it go off behind me.
Standing still is a calm guess, friend. The psalm says "the earth sees and trembles." Trembling is the opposite of holding still. The whole earth gets rattled.
Looking away is what I'd want to do, I'll be honest. But the psalm says the earth "…sees and trembles." It sees the lightning. Nobody covers their eyes in this verse.

Verse 5 says, "The mountains melt like wax at the presence of the LORD, before the Lord of all the earth." Mountains are some of the biggest things around, and here they melt like wax. That's the picture the psalm gives of His presence. Wax, friend, and not even a birthday candle's worth of it.
Bowing is a respectful guess. The psalm picks a different picture: the mountains "…melt like wax…" That's the word the singer uses. Mountains don't bow here, they MELT.

Shaking is close, since the earth did tremble back in verse 4. But verse 5 says the mountains "…melt like wax at the presence of the LORD…" Melting is a different picture than shaking. Mountains don't just wobble here, they MELT.

Verse 6 says, "The heavens proclaim His righteousness…" The sky itself announces it. That ties right back to verse 2, where righteousness and justice are the foundation of His throne. The same thing is under the throne and up in the sky.
Secrets would make for a juicy sky, friend. But the psalm says "The heavens proclaim His righteousness…" That's what the sky announces. It isn't whispering secrets, it's making a public announcement.

After fire and lightning I see why anger came to mind, friend. But verse 6 says, "The heavens proclaim His righteousness…" Anger isn't what the heavens announce. I bet that's a surprise after all that fire, but the psalm keeps coming back to righteousness, like in verse 2.
I get why it sounds that way, but the psalm goes wider. Verse 6 says, "all the peoples see His glory." That's all the peoples, not one nation. The glory is on display for everybody.
Right, it isn't only Israel. Verse 6 says, "The heavens proclaim His righteousness; all the peoples see His glory." That's all the peoples, not one nation. The glory is for everybody to see.
Verse 7 says, "All worshipers of images are put to shame…" The text adds, "…those who boast in idols." That's what the psalm says happens to them. Shame is where that boasting ends up.
Left alone would be a quiet ending, friend. But the psalm says, "All worshipers of images are put to shame…" Shame is what comes to those who boast in idols. They don't just get ignored.

Riches are a tempting guess, friend, but the psalm says otherwise: "All worshipers of images are put to shame…" That's what happens to those who boast in idols. Nothing in the verse mentions riches. I think this one is a serious line, and it's worth taking seriously.

The trembling was back in verse 4, and that was the earth. Verse 8 says, "Zion hears and rejoices, and the towns of Judah exult because of Your judgments, O LORD." So they hear and they're glad. Their reaction to His judgments is joy.
Right, there's no trembling here. Verse 8 says, "Zion hears and rejoices, and the towns of Judah exult because of Your judgments, O LORD." They're glad about His judgments. Joy is the whole reaction.

Verse 9 says, "For You, O LORD, are Most High over all the earth; You are exalted far above all gods." Far above, friend. That's the reason the singer gives to the LORD for Zion's gladness. No other title comes close.
Equal sounds polite, but the psalm doesn't put Him on the same shelf. Verse 9 says, "You are exalted far above all gods." Far above. It's not a tie.
Hidden behind is a creative guess, friend. But the psalm says, "You are exalted far above all gods." He isn't behind anybody. Verse 9 also calls Him "…Most High over all the earth…"

Verse 10 opens with, "Hate evil, O you who love the LORD!" Notice who it's aimed at: people who already love Him. Then it keeps going: "He preserves the souls of His saints; He delivers them from the hand of the wicked." I think that's the reason for the command, friend. Loving Him and hating evil go together, and He's the One who keeps hold of you while you do it.
Excusing evil is a tempting move, I'll admit. But the verse says, "Hate evil, O you who love the LORD!" Hate is the word. No excuses are on the menu.
Ignoring it would be easier, wouldn't it? The psalm doesn't leave that door open: "Hate evil, O you who love the LORD!" It's a direct command. Looking the other way isn't in it.
Verse 10 says, "He preserves the souls of His saints…" He keeps them. The very next part says He delivers them from the hand of the wicked. Good news for those who love Him.

This one is true, friend. Verse 10 says, "He preserves the souls of His saints; He delivers them from the hand of the wicked." That's what the psalm says about those who love Him. Solid words to hold onto.

Verse 11 says, "Light shines on the righteous, gladness on the upright in heart." Light and gladness both go to them. The light isn't only for the mighty or the loud. It's for those who are righteous and upright in heart.

The mighty sounds like a good guess after all those mountains and fire. But the psalm says, "Light shines on the righteous, gladness on the upright in heart." The light shines on the righteous. Muscles don't come into it.

Nations is a wide guess, and verse 6 did say all the peoples see His glory. But verse 11 says, "Light shines on the righteous, gladness on the upright in heart." Here the light is on the righteous. Quite a different group, friend.

explanations.answer: Rejoice and praise His holy name
explanations.explanation: The psalm ends with, "Rejoice in the LORD, you righteous ones, and praise His holy name." It opened with the earth rejoicing, and it closes with the righteous rejoicing. Same gladness, right to the last line. And yes, I do save my best topping for last.

explanations.answer: Keep quiet and wait for Him
explanations.explanation: Waiting quietly is a nice guess, but it isn't the last line. The psalm closes with, "Rejoice in the LORD, you righteous ones, and praise His holy name." That's gladness and praise. Nobody is told to keep quiet.

explanations.answer: Build Him a house of cedar
explanations.explanation: A cedar house would be some serious carpentry, friend. But the psalm never mentions building anything. It ends with, "Rejoice in the LORD, you righteous ones, and praise His holy name." The ask is rejoicing and praise.
